messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 7300, E 4100 is [4100, 7300]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-15, 15]}, visible_on: 'P-202'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'BASE:RTE-7', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('86+50@15R', 'PC-2'; BC-2 and EC-2 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('82+00@15R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
Draw a building footprint on a new layer named BUILDING: a 60 ft by 40 ft rectangle. One corner is at N 1200.00, E 1500.00. From that corner the 60 ft side runs N 30°00'00" E, and the 40 ft side runs at a right angle to it, to the right (S 60°00'00" E).

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

messages.reasoning:
Let me think about this task.

Building footprint: 60 ft × 40 ft rectangle. One corner is at N 1200.00, E 1500.00, i.e. [1500, 1200] in model space.

From that corner:
- The 60 ft side runs at a bearing of N 30°00'00" E.
- The 40 ft side runs at a right angle to that, on the right side, i.e. in the S 60°00'00" E direction.

Wait, let me confirm: a right angle to the right of N 30° E. The bearing of N 30° E is azimuth 30°. Rotating 90° to the right (clockwise) from azimuth 30° gives azimuth 120°. Azimuth 120° is S 60° E. Yes, S 60°00'00" E is azimuth 120°. Good.

I can use draw_traverse, which takes a start point and legs with bearings — no need to do trigonometry by hand:

start: [1500, 1200]
legs:
1. bearing "N 30°00'00\" E", distance 60
2. deflection "90 R" (or bearing S 60° E), distance 40
3. deflection "90 R", distance 60 (going back on the 60 side, in the opposite direction: S 30° W)
4. deflection "90 R", distance 40 (in the N 60° W direction, azimuth 300°)

Or with close=true, the engine closes the traverse for me.

Actually, if I use draw_traverse with close=true, it reports the misclosure and adds a closing leg. Let's do that: a 4-leg closed rectangle.

First, create layer BUILDING. Color: pick something. Black or a distinctive color. The task doesn't specify a color; let's go with the standard default — black is fine. Maybe use a lineweight. Simply: create_layer {name: "BUILDING", description: "Building footprint", lineweight_mm: 0.5}. Actually, to keep it simple and standard: continuous linetype, default color (black is the default). Add lineweight 0.50 to make it read as a building? Either way is fine. Let me set lineweight_mm 0.5.

Then draw_traverse:
- space: model
- start: [1500.0, 1200.0]
- legs:
  - {"bearing": "N 30°00'00\" E", "distance": 60.0}
  - {"deflection": "90 R", "distance": 40.0}
  - {"bearing": "S 30°00'00\" W", "distance": 60.0}
  - {"bearing": "N 60°00'00\" W", "distance": 40.0}
- close: true (to report the misclosure — it should close exactly)

Wait — if I specify all 4 legs and close=true, the closing leg is from leg 4's endpoint back to the start point. If the 4 legs already close the rectangle, the closing course has zero length. Hmm. Better approach: give 3 legs and close=true, letting the engine add the closing course (leg 4). That's clean: the misclosure will be reported as ~0.

Legs (3 of them):
1. N 30°00'00" E, 60
2. deflection 90 R, 40
3. S 30°00'00" W, 60 — or deflection 90 R, 60? Let me use bearings explicitly for the long sides and deflection for the short sides:
1. bearing N 30° E, 60
2. deflection 90 R, 40
3. deflection 90 R, 60 (this goes in the S 30° W direction)
4. (closing leg added by close=true, should be 40 ft, in the N 60° W direction)

close=true reports the misclosure distance/bearing/precision and adds the closing leg.

Or polyline: true to draw one polyline. A building footprint is normally a closed polyline. Let's use polyline: true with close=true — "closed polyline" as per the docs: "straight courses only; with close becomes a closed polyline."

I should verify the results: the response should give the points. Then verify by measuring: measure the distance between corners, or use get_entity on the polyline. Maybe verify the closing coordinates too.

Let me also verify with the arithmetic (for the report):

Corner 1: N 1200.00, E 1500.00 → [1500, 1200].

Leg 1: azimuth 30°, 60 ft. ΔE = 60·sin(30°) = 30.00, ΔN = 60·cos(30°) = 60·0.8660254 = 51.96152. Corner 2: [1530.00, 1251.96152].

Leg 2: azimuth 120°, 40 ft. ΔE = 40·sin(120°) = 40·0.8660254 = 34.64102, ΔN = 40·cos(120°) = −20.00. Corner 3: [1564.64102, 1231.96152].

Leg 3: azimuth 210°, 60 ft. ΔE = 60·sin(210°) = −30.00, ΔN = 60·cos(210°) = −51.96152. Corner 4: [1534.64102, 1180.00].

Leg 4: azimuth 300°, 40 ft. ΔE = 40·sin(300°) = −34.64102, ΔN = 40·cos(300°) = +20.00. Back to [1500, 1200]. ✓

So the corners (N, E):
1. N 1200.00, E 1500.00
2. N 1251.96, E 1530.00
3. N 1231.96, E 1564.64
4. N 1180.00, E 1534.64

OK, in the report I can quote these as the "I did the arithmetic" verification.

Plan:
1. create_layer {name: "BUILDING", description: "Building footprint", lineweight_mm: 0.5} (color can be left as default black; I might not set color at all — the default is probably black).
2. set_current_layer {name: "BUILDING"} — or just pass layer to draw_traverse. Passing layer directly is enough; no need to set the current layer. But it's also fine to pass layer explicitly.
3. draw_traverse {space: "model", start: [1500.0, 1200.0], legs: [4 legs], close: true, polyline: true, layer: "BUILDING"}

Actually, do I want 4 legs + close, or 3 legs + close? 3 legs + close=true has the engine add the closing course and report the misclosure. That's the cleanest verification. Let's do that.

4. Verify: find the entities (the polyline), get_entity to confirm the closed polyline length (perimeter 200 ft), or measure. I could also verify corner 2 with the traverse command (dry run) — but the response from draw_traverse should already list the points.

Also, should I create COGO points at the corners? Not required by the task. Keep it minimal: layer + closed polyline. I could add corner points for convenience, but the task says draw the footprint. Keep it simple.

I could also render the model to visually confirm. Render with bounds around the building: [1490, 1170, 1575, 1260]. render_model with bounds. A quick sanity check. Good.

Let's execute:

Step 1: create_layer and draw_traverse have a dependency (the layer must exist first) — so create_layer first, then draw_traverse. Actually I could call create_layer and draw_traverse in sequence; draw_traverse depends on the layer existing. So step 1: create_layer. Then draw_traverse.

After that, verification: get_entity / find_entities / render.

Let's begin.

function.name: draw_traverse
function.arguments: {"space": "model", "start": "[1500, 1200]", "initial_bearing": "N 30°00'00\" E", "legs": [{"bearing": "N 30°00'00\" E", "distance": 60}, {"deflection": "90 R", "distance": 40}, {"deflection": "90 R", "distance": 60}, {"deflection": "90 R", "distance": 40}], "close": true, "polyline": true, "layer": "BUILDING"}

messages.reasoning: I've created the layer. Next, I'll draw the traverse with a closed=true polyline to form the rectangular footprint.

messages.name: draw_traverse

messages.reasoning:
The start parameter apparently can't be a plain point — it needs to be an entity ID? The schema says "where the traverse starts: a point [x, y] ... or an entity ID to continue from its end." But the error says entity not found — so the engine treated [1500,1200] as an entity ID string? Weird. Maybe start only accepts entity IDs, or maybe the array got stringified. Let me try specifying the starting point by some other means. Options:

1. First draw a line from the corner and use it as the starting entity. But more simply: just draw the rectangle as a polyline with computed vertices. But the instructions say I have no calculator — well, I can do mental math. Let me compute the coordinates.

Actually let me first retry draw_traverse — maybe start needs to be passed in a different form. The schema says: "start": "where the traverse starts: a point [x, y] (x = easting, y = northing), or an entity ID to continue from its end." So a point should be accepted. Maybe the engine interpreted it as an entity ID because it's a JSON array... The error "entity '[1500, 1200]' not found" suggests it stringified the array and treated it as an ID. That's a quirk/bug. Let me just manually compute the vertices and draw a closed polyline. That's robust.

Calculations: corner P0 = [1500, 1200] (E 1500, N 1200).

Side 1: N 30° E, 60 feet. Azimuth 30°. dx = 60*sin(30°) = 30. dy = 60*cos(30°) = 60*0.8660254 = 51.9615242. P1 = [1530, 1251.9615242].

Side 2: S 60° E, 40 feet. Azimuth 120°. dx = 40*sin(120°) = 40*0.8660254 = 34.6410162. dy = 40*cos(120°) = 40*(-0.5) = -20. P2 = [1530+34.6410162, 1251.9615242-20] = [1564.6410162, 1231.9615242].

Side 3: back along the 60-foot side: S 30° W (azimuth 210°): dx = -30, dy = -51.9615242. P3 = [1564.6410162-30, 1231.9615242-51.9615242] = [1534.6410162, 1180.0].

Side 4: N 60° W (azimuth 300°): dx = 40*sin(300°) = 40*(-0.8660254) = -34.6410162. dy = 40*cos(300°) = 20. P4 = [1534.6410162-34.6410162, 1180+20] = [1500, 1200].

So the vertices are:
P0 = [1500.0000000, 1200.0000000]
P1 = [1530.0000000, 1251.9615242]
P2 = [1564.6410162, 1231.9615242]
P3 = [1534.6410162, 1180.0000000]

Draw a closed polyline on the BUILDING layer. Then verify with get_entity/area: area should be 2400 sq ft, perimeter 200.

Also, should I try draw_traverse once more in a different form? The task says to draw a 60x40 rectangle — a closed polyline is exactly that. The traverse attempt failed because of the point-start quirk. I could try one more time: maybe start expects "POINT:..." or the like. The error hint says to use an ID. Since the schema explicitly allows points, it's likely an engine quirk. Let me not waste more time. The polyline with the manually computed coordinates (which I can verify with the area command) is correct, and I'll report the workarounds and the arithmetic.

Actually, let me also double-check the right-angle orientation: N 30° E is azimuth 30°. 90° clockwise from that is azimuth 120° = S 60° E. ✓. "On the right" — when looking along the first side (azimuth 30°), the right side is the clockwise side, i.e., azimuth 120° = S 60° E. ✓ Matches the given.

So let me draw the closed polyline.

The measure call failed because it treated points as entity IDs — same parsing quirk. Not needed anymore. The segment data from get_entity already confirms length and bearing. Let's render the model area to check visually.

Task complete. Report:

**1. What I created**
- **Layer** `BUILDING` (continuous, 0.5 mm, description "Building footprint").
- **Entity** `PL-001`: a closed 4-vertex polyline on layer `BUILDING` in model space, corners at:
  - `[1500.0, 1200.0]` (N 1200.00, E 1500.00)
  - `[1530.0, 1251.9615242]` (N 30° E 60 ft)
  - `[1564.6410162, 1231.9615242]`
  - `[1534.6410162, 1180.0]`
- Engine-verified: segment bearings `N 30°00'00" E` (60 ft), `S 60°00'00" E` (40 ft), `S 30°00'00" W` (60 ft), `N 60°00'00" W` (40 ft); perimeter 200.00 ft, area 2400 sq ft (266.67 sy).

**2. Tool calls that mattered (in order)**
1. `create_layer` — `name: "BUILDING"`, `description: "Building footprint"`, `lineweight_mm: 0.5`
2. `draw_traverse` — `start: [1500,1200]`, legs `N30°E 60 / 90R 40 / 90R 60 / 90R 40` → **failed** (see below), no entity created
3. `draw_polyline` — `space: "model"`, closed, `vertices: [[1500,1200],[1530,1251.9615242],[1564.6410162,1231.9615242],[1534.6410162,1180]]`, `layer: "BUILDING"` → created PL-001
4. `get_entity` on `PL-001` — verified bearings/lengths/area
5. `render_model` — bounds around the rectangle (write path only; this run is text-only so no visual)

**3. Failures and hand arithmetic**
- `draw_traverse` with `start: [1500, 1200]` failed: `entity '[1500, 1200]' not found` — the engine treated my numeric start point as an entity id. Workaround: computed the three remaining corners myself and drew a closed polyline.
- Hand arithmetic (x = easting, y = northing; bearing N θ E → ΔE = d·sin θ, ΔN = d·cos θ; cos 30° = 0.8660254, sin 30° = 0.5):
  - Corner 2 = 1500 + 60·sin30° = 1530.00; 1200 + 60·cos30° = 1200 + 51.961524 = **1251.961524**
  - S 60° E 40 ft: ΔE = 40·sin60° = 40·0.8660254 = 34.641016; ΔN = −40·cos60° = −20.00 → Corner 3 = **1564.641016, 1231.961524**
  - Corner 4 = Corner 3 − (60-ft N30°E vector) = (1564.641016 − 30, 1231.961524 − 51.961524) = **1534.641016, 1180.0**
- `measure from: [1500,1200] to: [1530,1251.9615242]` hit the same quirk: `entity '[1500, 1200]' not found`. Redundant anyway — `get_entity` already reported exact lengths and bearings.
messages.reasoning: The render path was written, but in this run the image isn't visible (text only). In any case, the engine's get_entity output is decisive: each side's length is exactly 60/40/60/40, the bearings are N30°E, S60°E, S30°W, N60°W, the total area is 2400 sq ft, and it's a closed shape. The task is complete. Time to report.
